doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

title: Learning from records at the Vipers and by ear
summary: He listens to big-band records on neighborhood jukeboxes and at a dancehall with a homemade sound system, and learns tunes by ear with a retentive memory.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Well, at the time, I was listening to a whole lot of music -- records -- almost in every neighborhood they had little penny vendors, little restaurants, you walked past, and you could hear all the music you want. Basie, Benny Goodman, Slam Stewart, Slim and Slam ... oh my God, so many good musicians -- naturally Duke was at the top.
Pops. Oh, boy, Chick Webb with Ella.

Oh ... there was a club, not a club, but a little place, a little dancehall -- like I said, I wasn't quite 14, and I was working in this club, and it was a little dancehall right down the 30th block on Cosgrove called The Vipers. Now, it was run by an old man they called Pop Pearson and his son, Charlie. Well, Charlie had -- to me, I

believe that was the first stereo -- he made a vendor, and played records -- he had about 6 or 7 loud speakers, and he built it, and he'd sit up there and work the controls, and he knew all the arrangements, these big bands, and certain bands he would turn it up, you know, turn the volume up, and oh, it was so beautiful -- it was just like being -- sitting up close to a big band.

And so I'm just listening -- that's when I first heard of "Jack the Bear" with Duke Ellington and Blanton. And so I knew a whole lot of the arrangements, and I knew a whole lot of tunes, just by listening. And the little 5 piece band I'm working with, we would play them -- "Jumping at the Woodside" and "One o'Clock Jump" -- even things the Ceford band was playing. Lanceford Luntzwood was very popular.
I've heard Eubie Blake and Earl Hines talk about learning music by listening, and how you have almost a photographic memory. All these tunes, it seems phenomenal, but that's how you learn.

You learn and you retain those tunes, you know? You never forget them. I mean, you might not play a tune for a year, but somebody will say, "Do you know so and so" - and he'll call the name; you can't remember the name, but as soon as he plays at least 3 or 4 bars, you know it and you can play it.
